subject: Structure of the precision matrix of JRSS paper's disease mapping example

messages.author: 26c06a219175f2cf
messages.subject: Structure of the precision matrix of JRSS paper's disease mapping example
parts:
Hi,

I am trying to reproduce the example 5.4 of the Rue&Martino&Chopin's JRSS paper about cancer incidence (the data seems to be available in INLA package).

Before even trying to figure out how to actually code this up with INLA, I started to wonder how the joint prior precision matrix of the model is computed? In the paper it says that it has dimension of 216 × 15 + 1 = 3241, where 216 is the number of spatial districts, 15 is the number of age groups and 1 is the common intercept. Comparing this with the example in the INLA review paper on https://arxiv.org/pdf/1604.00860.pdf, I don't understand where does this come from? Based on the review paper and my initial intuition I would have assumed the dimensions to be something like 216 (spatial random effect) + 216 (smooth spatial effect) + 15 + 1. Is there some sort of nesting going on or what?

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Structure of the precision matrix of JRSS paper's disease mapping example
parts:
Without checking either paper's details, a simple explanation could be
that it's not the same model? A space-and-age interaction model would
have 216 x 15 elements. A purely "main effects" model in space and age
would have 216 + 15. So double check if the two text are actually
discussing identical models. But then there are other issues, like how
the models are represented inside R-INLA. Haavards suggestion to have
a look at the 2005 Rue&Held GMRF book is good; many things are
explained there.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Structure of the precision matrix of JRSS paper's disease mapping example
parts:
Thanks,

Yes the models are different, I was trying to understand the logic behind the general construction. I though the "summation of precision matrices" strategy of Section 2.4 of the "Bayesian Computing with INLA: A Review" paper was the general strategy, but when reading more carefully, this seems to be the general strategy for additive "main effects" model, whereas I guess the disease mapping example in the other paper has interactions as well (which I didn't understand based on the text). Same model seem to be also in the GMRF book, so I'll check that as well.

Jouni
